newsitem.title: USA: U.S. study links mental health with substance abuse.
newsitem.headline: U.S. study links mental health with substance abuse.

text.p: Teenagers with emotional or behavioural problems are more likely to use marijuana or become addicted to alcohol and tobacco than those who are stable, a new report released on Friday showed.

Adults who have suffered depression, anxiety disorders, panic attacks, or agoraphobia were about twice as likely to have been dependent on cigarettes and several times more likely to have been dependent on illegal drugs in the past year than those who who were free of those syndromes.

The findings, published on Friday by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, are part of the first report on mental health data collected in a continuing national survey on drug abuse.

"This report represents an important step in the measurement of the relationship of mental health to substance use, abuse, and dependence in the general population," said the agency's administrator Nelba Chavez.

Bernard Arons, director of SAMHSA's Centre for Mental Health Services, said that too often early warning signs of psychosocial problems in adolescents were overlooked or attributed to "growing pains," but those problems could lead to substance abuse in later years.

Among an estimated 22 million children aged 12 to 17 in 1994, 4.2 million had problem scores indicating high levels of psychosocial problems during the past six months, the report said, noting there were no significant differences based on race, ethnicity, population density, or region.

An estimated 1 million, or 4.8 percent, of all adolescents received outpatient mental health treatment for problems such as depression, anxiety, social withdrawal, attention problems, delinquent behaviour and aggressive behaviour.
Teen boys were more likely to use substances than teen girls, but among teens with high problem scores, girls were just as likely as boys to binge drink, smoke cigarettes or use illicit drugs.

SAMHSA, an agency of the Department of Health and Human Services, is the federal government's leading agency for improving the quality and availability of substance abuse prevention, addiction treatment and mental health services.
